title: After Years in America, an NRI Came Home — and Felt He Didn't Belong
excerpt: NDTV reported the account of an NRI who moved back after years in the United States and now describes loneliness and disconnection: "I feel like I don't belong here." The story reflects a wider, often unspoken strain among returning Indians.
body:
• NDTV reported the account of an NRI who returned to India after years in the United States and now describes feeling lonely and out of place: "I feel like I don't belong here."
  • The account echoes a wider pattern of "reverse culture shock" among returning Indians — job-market anxiety, workplace adjustment, and a homecoming that doesn't match the imagined reunion.
  • An HSBC survey found about a third of Indians abroad don't feel "like a local" in their host country — yet many discover that belonging proves elusive at home too.
  • For NRIs weighing a return, fellow returnees and therapists advise preparing for the emotional landing, not just the logistics: income, privacy, and realistic expectations.

After years in the United States, an NRI came home to India expecting a reunion. Instead, according to an account reported by NDTV on September 20, it has felt like exile in reverse — loneliness, restlessness, and a blunt admission: "I feel like I don't belong here." Home in theory, foreign in practice: surrounded by family, yet unable to shake the feeling of being an outsider.

Reverse culture shock is real

Psychologists call it reverse culture shock: the disorientation of returning to a familiar place that has quietly become strange. Mint reported the case of a Redditor who returned to India after four years in the UK when a graduate visa ran out. Two weeks after landing, the person wrote that life abroad had become their comfort zone — "my routine, my friends, the places I used to go" — while the Indian job market felt "terrible," feeding a loop of anxiety and indecision.

"Even in my own home with family around, I feel restless and disconnected."

— a returnee quoted by Mint

A YouTuber documenting his own return lists what piled up after the excitement faded: nosy relatives, unstable income, traffic, pollution, a lack of privacy, family expectations — and missing parts of America. It made him realise that "returning to India is not the same as going back to your old life."

The workplace whiplash

Work is where many returnees feel the shock most sharply. Mint reported the account of a 26-year-old finance professional, schooled in Singapore and London, whose employer's restructuring landed her in a lower-paying India role. Three months in, she described "boss culture," office politics, and a "lack of boundaries" that left her mentally exhausted. "I miss the openness, the structure, and the respect for boundaries," she wrote — adding that she now has to justify taking a day off, something she never faced abroad.

A senior NRI executive who spent more than 15 years in the United States and Switzerland described a related friction to VisaVerge: not the roads or the paperwork, but a sense that the rules of the game had changed. "In India, no matter how much I work, the game feels rigged against me," he wrote. "This... is killing my ambition."

Belonging proves elusive in both directions

The paradox: many returnees left partly because they never fully felt they belonged abroad — and came home to find belonging had changed shape. An HSBC survey found about 33% of Indians overseas did not agree they "feel like a local" in their host country, with nearly 31% unsure. A researcher at the Australian National University said loneliness and mental health struggles among Indian students abroad "remain unheard."

Life coach Maitri Shah, who spent seven years in the US before returning, describes a similar arc: loneliness and anxiety abroad, a slow professional rebuild, and a move home that felt like arrival at herself. She now works as a counseling psychologist in India.

Why the return wave keeps growing

None of this has slowed the tide. Green card backlogs, H-1B uncertainty, and the cost of American life keep pushing skilled Indians toward repatriation, while India's job market makes the move more viable than a decade ago. A recent viral video about an H-1B tech worker returning despite a heavy loan — he "could no longer bear the loneliness" — drew thousands of sympathetic responses.

For the diaspora, the account is a caution against romanticising either side of the ocean. India offers what America often can't: family within reach, familiar rhythms. What it doesn't offer is a time machine — the country kept moving, and returnees come back as different people to a different place.

What a softer landing looks like

Returnees who stuck it out give the same advice: secure income before the move; set boundaries with family early; give the adjustment a full year. Reverse culture shock typically peaks a few months in — right when the novelty wears off. Online returnee communities, from Reddit's r/returnToIndia to YouTube comment sections, have become informal support groups for the disoriented.

Belonging, the NDTV account suggests, is not a place you return to. It's something you rebuild — slowly, and on the second try, with clearer eyes.
image_caption: Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport in Mumbai. After years in America, one NRI came home — and found he no longer felt he belonged.
nri_angle: For NRIs weighing a return, this story underscores that repatriation is an emotional transition as much as a logistical one — belonging must be rebuilt, not just revisited.
author: Diaspora Desk
